questions.prompt: What is the weighting of this brain scan?
questions.explain: Short TR (500 ms) and short TE (12 ms) give T1 weighting — fat/white matter bright, CSF dark.

questions.prompt: And the weighting of this one?
questions.explain: Long TR (4000 ms) and long TE (100 ms) give T2 weighting — fluid (CSF) is bright.

questions.prompt: Long TR but short TE — what weighting is this?
questions.explain: Long TR removes T1 weighting and short TE removes T2 weighting — what's left is proton-density: signal tracks tissue water content (grey > white, CSF intermediate).

questions.prompt: Which sequence is this — note the dark CSF in the ventricles despite the T2-like brightness elsewhere?
questions.explain: Heavily T2-weighted but with CSF nulled by a long TI (~2500 ms) = FLAIR — the workhorse for periventricular lesions.

questions.prompt: This image shows bright vessels with no contrast injection. What technique produced it?
questions.explain: Time-of-flight (TOF) MRA relies on inflow enhancement — fresh unsaturated blood entering the slice is bright against saturated stationary tissue. No contrast needed.

questions.prompt: A bright focus appears on this diffusion-weighted image of an acute-stroke patient. What does restricted diffusion most likely indicate here?
questions.explain: Restricted diffusion (bright DWI / dark ADC) is the hallmark of an acute infarct — cytotoxic oedema traps water. Always confirm on the ADC map to exclude T2 shine-through.

questions.prompt: Which sequence is best for detecting microhaemorrhages and iron, like the dark foci shown here?
questions.explain: SWI exploits the strong susceptibility of blood products / iron / calcium — they bloom dark. It is the most sensitive sequence for microbleeds and mineralisation.

questions.prompt: A mass enhances brightly on this post-gadolinium T1 scan. Why does gadolinium make it bright?
options: Gadolinium shortens T1 where it leaks through a broken blood-brain barrier
questions.explain: Gadolinium is paramagnetic — it shortens nearby T1, so tissue brightens on T1-weighting. It only reaches the extravascular space where the blood-brain barrier is broken, so enhancement marks BBB breakdown (tumour, active inflammation).

questions.prompt: This is a quantitative perfusion map. A mass shows markedly RAISED values here. Which map is it, and what does that suggest?
options: CBV — high CBV suggests a high-grade tumour
questions.explain: This is the DSC cerebral blood VOLUME map. A tumour grows leaky neovasculature, so raised CBV is a marker of high tumour grade.

questions.prompt: On this DCE permeability map, normal brain is dark but a lesion enhances brightly. What is being measured, and why does normal brain stay dark?
options: Ktrans — the intact blood-brain barrier blocks leakage
CBF — normal brain has no flow
questions.explain: Ktrans is the volume transfer constant (permeability). An intact blood-brain barrier keeps contrast intravascular (Ktrans≈0); tumour/active-lesion vessels leak, so they light up.

questions.prompt: This brain scan shows faint repeating copies of the head across the image. What artifact is this, and along which direction does it propagate?
options: Motion ghosting — along the phase-encode direction
questions.explain: Periodic motion (respiration, pulsation) produces discrete ghosts spaced along the PHASE-ENCODE axis. Averaging (NEX), triggering, or breath-holding reduces them.

questions.prompt: This long-TE gradient-echo image loses signal near the skull base and air interfaces. What causes it, and how do you reduce it?
options: Susceptibility — use spin echo or a shorter TE
questions.explain: Susceptibility differences at air/bone/tissue boundaries dephase spins — worst on long-TE gradient echo. A spin echo's 180° pulse refocuses the dephasing, and a shorter TE gives less time to dephase.

questions.prompt: At this fat–water boundary in the knee there is a dark/bright misregistration band along the readout. What is it, and the fix?
options: Chemical shift — raise the receiver bandwidth (or fat-suppress)
questions.explain: Fat and water resonate ~3.5 ppm apart, so they map to slightly different readout positions — a shift at fat–water borders. A higher receiver bandwidth (or fat suppression) shrinks it.

questions.prompt: On this knee scan the fatty marrow is suppressed (dark). Which fat-suppression technique uses an inversion pulse timed to null fat?
questions.explain: STIR uses a 180° inversion with a TI (~150–200 ms at 1.5T) chosen so fat crosses zero signal. It is robust to B0 inhomogeneity, but also nulls anything with fat-like T1 — so it is avoided after gadolinium.

questions.prompt: This sequence gives bright fluid and blood with T2/T1 contrast and a very fast acquisition. Which is it?
questions.explain: Balanced steady-state free precession (bSSFP / TrueFISP / FIESTA) gives high SNR with T2/T1 contrast — bright blood and fluid — used in cardiac and fetal imaging. It is prone to off-resonance banding.

questions.prompt: A gradient-echo image at a long TE. What is its dominant weighting?
questions.explain: Gradient echo has no 180° refocusing pulse, so signal decays by T2* (which includes susceptibility dephasing). A long-TE gradient echo is T2*-weighted — sensitive to blood products and iron.

questions.prompt: Multiple ovoid periventricular lesions are bright on this FLAIR scan. What is the classic diagnosis?
questions.explain: Ovoid periventricular/callosal lesions bright on FLAIR (often perpendicular to the ventricles — 'Dawson's fingers') are the hallmark of multiple sclerosis.

questions.prompt: The infarct that was bright on DWI is also DARK on this ADC map. What does the dark ADC confirm?
questions.explain: Always pair DWI with ADC: genuine restriction is DARK on ADC. If the lesion were bright on ADC, the DWI signal would be T2 shine-through, not true restriction.

questions.prompt: This perfusion map was made with NO contrast injection — grey matter is bright, white matter dark. Which technique?
questions.explain: ASL magnetically labels arterial blood as an endogenous tracer — no contrast. Its CBF map shows grey matter perfused ~2–3× white matter.

questions.prompt: On this MTT map a territory shows markedly PROLONGED transit time. In acute stroke, what does that region represent?
questions.explain: Prolonged MTT marks tissue whose blood arrives slowly — hypoperfused territory. Combined with CBV it separates the infarct core (low CBV) from salvageable penumbra (preserved CBV, long MTT).

questions.prompt: On this CBF map an area is strikingly DARK. What does reduced cerebral blood flow there indicate?
questions.explain: A dark region on CBF = reduced blood flow = ischaemia. In stroke the core has the lowest CBF; a perfusion–diffusion mismatch estimates salvageable tissue.

questions.prompt: A bright stripe of noise runs across this image as a fixed line. What artifact is it, and the usual cause?
options: Zipper — stray RF entering the scan room
questions.explain: A zipper is a line of alternating bright/dark pixels from stray radiofrequency (a leaky door seal, electronics) reaching the receiver. Restoring RF shielding removes it.

questions.prompt: This image is geometrically warped, worse toward the edges. What causes it?
questions.explain: Real gradients become nonlinear away from isocentre, so anatomy is spatially warped toward the periphery of the field of view. Vendor distortion correction (and keeping anatomy near isocentre) mitigates it.

questions.prompt: Which imaging plane is this brain slice?
questions.explain: A coronal slice — viewed from the front, dividing anterior from posterior. The orbits, temporal lobes and the full vertical span of the ventricles come into view.

questions.prompt: And which plane is this one?
questions.explain: A sagittal slice — a side-on cut dividing left from right; the corpus callosum, brainstem and cerebellum line up in profile (a midline sagittal is the classic view of these).

questions.prompt: On this knee scan, joint fluid and the cartilage stand out bright while marrow fat is darker. What weighting is this?
questions.explain: Long TR (4000 ms) and long TE (90 ms) give T2 weighting — fluid is bright, so effusions, cartilage defects and meniscal tears (fluid tracking into a tear) are conspicuous.

questions.prompt: Here the fatty marrow and subcutaneous fat are bright while joint fluid is dark. What weighting is this knee scan?
questions.explain: Short TR (500 ms) and short TE (12 ms) give T1 weighting — fat (and fatty marrow) is bright, fluid is dark. T1 is the anatomy/marrow workhorse.

questions.prompt: Diffusion, perfusion and fMRI all rely on a very fast single-shot readout that fills the whole slice after one excitation — fast, but prone to distortion and susceptibility dropout. What is that readout called?
questions.explain: Echo-planar imaging (EPI) samples all of k-space after a single excitation — the speed enabler for diffusion, dynamic perfusion and fMRI BOLD — at the cost of geometric distortion and susceptibility dropout near air.

questions.prompt: A spoiled gradient-echo with a short TE and a high flip angle (70°). What weighting dominates?
questions.explain: In spoiled gradient echo the flip angle drives T1 weighting (a high flip gives more T1 contrast), and a short TE avoids T2* decay. This is the basis of fast 3D T1 volumes (e.g. spoiled-GRE / MPRAGE-type scans).

questions.prompt: Raising the b-value from 0 to 1000 s/mm² makes this image more sensitive to what?
options: The random motion of water molecules (diffusion)
questions.explain: The b-value sets the diffusion sensitisation: higher b weights more strongly for water mobility. Tissue where water is restricted (e.g. an acute infarct) stays bright as b increases.

questions.prompt: This ring-shaped lesion shows CENTRAL restricted diffusion (a bright core on DWI). What does that favour?
questions.explain: Thick, viscous pus restricts diffusion, so a pyogenic abscess shows a bright (restricted) centre on DWI. A necrotic tumour cavity usually does NOT restrict centrally — a key way to tell them apart.

questions.prompt: A focal white-matter lesion is obvious on FLAIR but easy to miss on plain T2 near the ventricles. Why does FLAIR help?
options: It nulls CSF, so periventricular lesions are not masked by bright fluid
questions.explain: FLAIR is heavily T2-weighted but nulls CSF with a long TI. Lesions sitting next to the ventricles are no longer hidden by bright CSF — the reason FLAIR is the screen for periventricular disease.

questions.prompt: Around this mass, finger-like T2 hyperintensity spreads through the surrounding white matter. What is it?
options: Vasogenic oedema tracking along white-matter pathways
questions.explain: A leaky tumour drives vasogenic oedema that spreads through the white matter (sparing cortex), bright on T2/FLAIR. Surrounding oedema out of proportion to a lesion is a clue to an underlying mass.

questions.prompt: DSC perfusion follows a gadolinium bolus through the brain. What signal change does the passing bolus cause?
options: A transient T2* signal DROP from susceptibility as the bolus passes
questions.explain: In Dynamic Susceptibility Contrast the concentrated bolus causes a brief T2* signal dip; the depth and timing of that dip across the passage are fitted to CBV, CBF and MTT.

questions.prompt: A patient with poor renal function needs perfusion imaging but cannot receive gadolinium. Which method fits?
questions.explain: ASL magnetically labels arterial blood as an endogenous tracer — no exogenous contrast — so it is the perfusion method of choice when gadolinium is contraindicated.

questions.prompt: These ghosts repeat along the phase-encode axis from patient motion. Which option does NOT help reduce them?
options: Swapping the phase- and frequency-encode directions
questions.explain: Motion ghosts are tamed by triggering/breath-holding, averaging, motion correction, or swapping the phase direction to throw ghosts off the anatomy of interest. Increasing TE does nothing for motion (it tends to worsen other problems).

questions.prompt: Chemical-shift artifact at fat–water borders is worse at 3T than at 1.5T. Why?
options: The fat–water frequency difference (in Hz) is larger at higher field
questions.explain: The fat–water shift is fixed at ~3.5 ppm, so in Hz it doubles from 1.5T to 3T — a larger pixel misregistration for the same receiver bandwidth. Raise the bandwidth (or fat-suppress) to shrink it.

questions.prompt: Which imaging plane is this brain slice?
questions.explain: An axial (transverse) slice — it divides superior from inferior and shows both hemispheres symmetrically, with the lateral ventricles and basal ganglia in cross-section.

questions.prompt: Which plane of the knee is this — the view that shows the cruciate ligaments and the menisci in profile?
questions.explain: Sagittal — the side-on plane along the ACL/PCL and through the meniscal body, the standard plane for assessing the cruciates and meniscal tears.

questions.prompt: This long side-on image stacks the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs. Which region and plane is it?
questions.explain: A sagittal spine image — vertebral bodies, discs and the spinal cord line up vertically. Sagittal is the default survey plane for the spine.

questions.prompt: Which plane best displays the corpus callosum along its whole length (genu, body and splenium)?
questions.explain: The corpus callosum is a midline C-shaped band, so a midline sagittal shows it end-to-end. Axial and coronal slices only cut it in fragments.

questions.prompt: Which body region is this examination — femoral condyles, tibial plateau and the joint space?
questions.explain: The knee — femoral condyles above, tibial plateau below, the patella anteriorly, and the menisci and cruciate ligaments within the joint.

questions.prompt: This angiogram encodes flow as velocity-dependent phase shifts and can be tuned to a velocity range (VENC). Which technique is it?
questions.explain: Phase-contrast MRA uses bipolar gradients so moving spins accrue phase proportional to velocity (set by the VENC). It yields flow speed AND direction — unlike time-of-flight, which relies on inflow brightness.

questions.prompt: With the b-value set to 0, a diffusion scan carries no diffusion sensitisation. What weighting does it then resemble — the basis of 'T2 shine-through'?
questions.explain: A b=0 image is essentially T2-weighted. So a lesion that is bright on high-b DWI purely because it is T2-bright (not truly restricting) is 'T2 shine-through' — always confirm with the ADC map.

questions.prompt: Why does a gradient echo decay by T2* while a spin echo decays by the slower T2?
options: The spin echo's 180° refocusing pulse reverses static field dephasing
The gradient echo uses a longer TR
questions.explain: A spin echo's 180° pulse refocuses dephasing from static field inhomogeneity (T2'), leaving pure T2. A gradient echo has no such pulse, so it keeps that extra dephasing — T2* = T2 plus susceptibility/inhomogeneity. That makes GRE sensitive to blood products and iron.

questions.prompt: On this T2*-weighted gradient-echo scan, small old bleeds appear as dark 'blooming' foci. Why does GRE reveal them when spin echo may not?
options: GRE keeps susceptibility dephasing (no 180° refocusing), so blood products bloom
questions.explain: Without a 180° refocusing pulse, the strong susceptibility of haemosiderin/blood products dephases spins and 'blooms' dark on GRE (and even more on SWI). A spin echo refocuses that dephasing and can hide microbleeds.

questions.prompt: Multiple sclerosis plaques are bright on FLAIR. On this T1 scan a plaque appears DARK (a 'black hole'). What does that indicate?
questions.explain: Persistent T1-hypointense 'black holes' mark chronic, destructive demyelination with axonal loss — a marker of disease severity beyond simple lesion counting on FLAIR.

questions.prompt: After gadolinium this tumour shows a bright enhancing rim around a non-enhancing centre. What does the non-enhancing core most likely represent?
questions.explain: The enhancing rim is viable, vascularised tumour with a broken blood-brain barrier; the non-enhancing core is necrosis. A pyogenic abscess can look similar — DWI separates them, because pus restricts diffusion centrally.

questions.prompt: On this ASL cerebral-blood-flow map, grey matter is brighter than white matter. Why?
options: Grey matter receives ~2–3× the blood flow of white matter
questions.explain: Cortical grey matter is perfused about 2–3× more than white matter, so it is brighter on a CBF map. ASL measures this quantitatively using magnetically labelled blood — no contrast.

questions.prompt: Which dynamic perfusion method tracks contrast leakage on T1-weighting over minutes to measure permeability (Ktrans)?
questions.explain: DCE acquires T1-weighted images over minutes and models contrast leaking into the extravascular space → Ktrans (permeability). DSC is the fast first-pass T2* method that yields CBV/CBF/MTT.

questions.prompt: Near a metallic implant the image shows signal voids and geometric warping. Which choice REDUCES this susceptibility artifact?
options: Spin echo with a short TE and high receiver bandwidth
Doing nothing — it cannot be reduced
questions.explain: Susceptibility near metal is worst on long-TE gradient echo. A spin echo's 180° pulse refocuses the dephasing; a short TE and high bandwidth (plus dedicated metal-artifact-reduction sequences) shrink the voids and distortion.

questions.prompt: Which body region is this axial scan — liver, spleen, both kidneys and bowel loops?
questions.explain: The abdomen — liver and spleen, both kidneys and bowel; the axial plane is the survey workhorse for abdominal anatomy.

questions.prompt: Which region is this axial scan, centred on the bladder with the pelvic bones and musculature around it?
questions.explain: The pelvis — the bladder centrally, the bony pelvis and the pelvic floor/gluteal musculature; in practice the reproductive organs and rectum are the targets.

questions.prompt: Which plane is best for comparing the two hippocampi side-by-side (e.g. when looking for mesial temporal sclerosis)?
questions.explain: A coronal plane (perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus) shows both hippocampi symmetrically for direct left-vs-right comparison — the standard view for mesial temporal sclerosis.

questions.prompt: On this knee scan the TR is long but the TE is short — high-signal, intermediate contrast that shows cartilage and menisci well. What weighting is it?
questions.explain: Long TR + short TE = proton-density: high SNR with intermediate contrast. With fat suppression it is the MSK workhorse for cartilage and menisci.

questions.prompt: In an inversion-recovery sequence, what sets which tissue is nulled (appears darkest)?
options: The inversion time (TI) relative to that tissue's T1
questions.explain: A tissue is nulled when TI ≈ 0.69 × its T1 (its longitudinal magnetisation crosses zero). A short TI (~150–200 ms) nulls fat (STIR); a long TI (~2000–2500 ms) nulls CSF (FLAIR).

questions.prompt: STIR uses a short TI (~150 ms) and FLAIR a long TI (~2500 ms). What does each one null?
options: STIR nulls fat; FLAIR nulls CSF
STIR nulls CSF; FLAIR nulls fat
questions.explain: The null follows TI ≈ 0.69 × T1: a short TI matches fat's short T1 (STIR → dark fat), a long TI matches CSF's long T1 (FLAIR → dark CSF).

questions.prompt: Holding TR long, you LENGTHEN the echo time (TE). Which way does the contrast move?
questions.explain: TE controls T2 weighting — a longer TE lets long-T2 tissue (fluid) stay bright while short-T2 tissue decays. (TR controls T1 weighting; a long TR removes it.)

questions.prompt: This infarct is bright on DWI but is still NOT visible on FLAIR. What does that DWI–FLAIR mismatch suggest about timing?
options: It is not a stroke at all
questions.explain: DWI turns positive within minutes; FLAIR lags by hours. A DWI-positive but FLAIR-negative infarct is therefore early — a marker used to select unknown-onset strokes for thrombolysis.

questions.prompt: Days after onset this infarct has become bright on FLAIR (it was already bright on DWI from the start). What changed to make it show here?
options: Vasogenic oedema raised the tissue water and T2
questions.explain: Over hours-to-days vasogenic oedema increases tissue water and T2, so the infarct brightens on T2/FLAIR — while DWI was positive from the first minutes (cytotoxic oedema).

questions.prompt: In acute stroke the DWI lesion is small but the MTT perfusion abnormality is much larger. What does this 'mismatch' represent?
questions.explain: The diffusion lesion approximates the irreversible core; the larger perfusion deficit also includes hypoperfused-but-viable penumbra. A big diffusion–perfusion mismatch means more tissue to save with reperfusion.

questions.prompt: Which plane of the knee is this — the cross-section through the patellofemoral joint?
questions.explain: Axial — looking down through the knee; the patella in the trochlear groove (the patellofemoral joint) and the retinacula are assessed in this plane.

questions.prompt: Which plane shows the medial and lateral collateral ligaments and the meniscal bodies side-to-side?
questions.explain: Coronal — a front-on plane that lays out both collateral ligaments and the meniscal bodies from side to side.

questions.prompt: Which body region is this axial scan — heart and great vessels centrally, lungs to the sides?
questions.explain: The thorax — the heart and great vessels in the mediastinum centrally, with the lungs laterally; axial is the standard survey plane.

questions.prompt: Which single plane best shows the brainstem continuing into the cervical spinal cord?
questions.explain: A midline sagittal lines up the midbrain, pons, medulla and the cervicomedullary junction into the cord — the survey view of the craniocervical junction.

questions.prompt: Same slice and sequence — what changed from A to B?
options: The echo time (TE) was lengthened — now T2-weighted
questions.explain: Only TE changed (12 → 100 ms), TR stayed long. The long TE lets CSF (long T2) go bright — B is T2-weighted while A is proton-density.

questions.prompt: Same slice and sequence — what changed from A to B?
options: The repetition time (TR) was shortened — now T1-weighted
questions.explain: Only TR changed (4000 → 500 ms), TE stayed short. The short TR adds T1 weighting — B is T1 (CSF dark) while A is proton-density.

questions.prompt: Same T2 knee, same plane — what changed from A to B?
options: Fat suppression was switched on — the bright fat is now dark
questions.explain: The only change is fat suppression. The bright subcutaneous/marrow fat in A is nulled in B, so fluid and oedema (e.g. a bone bruise) stand out — the basis of fluid-sensitive MSK imaging.

questions.prompt: Same T1 slice of a brain tumour — what changed from A to B?
options: Gadolinium was given — the lesion now enhances
questions.explain: Same T1 sequence; gadolinium was administered for B. The newly bright (enhancing) tissue marks where the blood-brain barrier is broken.

questions.prompt: Same slice in a patient with microhaemorrhages — what changed from A to B?
options: Switched to a susceptibility sequence (SWI) — the bleeds now bloom dark
questions.explain: B is SWI: the strong susceptibility of blood products blooms into dark foci that the T1 spin echo in A barely shows. SWI/GRE are far more sensitive to microbleeds.

questions.prompt: Same T1 brain, same sequence — what changed from A to B?
questions.explain: Same T1 spin echo and weighting; only the slice orientation changed — A is axial (both hemispheres in cross-section), B is coronal (front-on).
